message.content:
**Short‑answer:**  
Painting the entire Eiffel Tower from start to finish typically takes **about one year**, though only the “actual” spray‑painting itself lasts a few weeks once everything else—clean‑up, primer, protective coatings, permits, scaffolds, and safety checks—is already in place.

---

### Why it’s so long?

| Step | What happens | Typical duration |
|------|--------------|------------------|
| **Planning & permitting** | Engineers design the job, choose pigments, calculate material needs, secure city/Parisian heritage approvals, coordinate traffic closures, and set up safety protocols. | 3–6 months |
| **Surface prep** | Workers remove old paint layers, clean rusted metal, sandblast, treat corrosion, and prime the steel. Because the tower is exposed to wind, rain, and pollution, this step is meticulous. | 2–4 weeks per section – total ≈ 3–5 months |
| **Coating application** | A team of painters applies the new color using high‑pressure sprayers mounted on mobile platforms or fixed ladders/scaffolds. Weather windows (no rain, low humidity) limit daily working hours. | 2–4 weeks per section – total ≈ 2–3 months |
| **Inspection & touch‑ups** | Inspectors check adhesion, coverage, and compliance with preservation standards. Minor corrections follow. | 1–2 weeks |
| **Cleanup & restoration** | Remove temporary structures, restore surrounding areas, re‑install signage, and conduct post‑job inspections. | 1–2 weeks |

> *Note:* These figures assume a single dedicated crew operating continuously under favorable weather. In reality, Paris often schedules the work during winter when fewer tourists visit, which adds logistical constraints.

---

### Historical Context

* **1979–1980 Refurbishment** – Took roughly two calendar years from kickoff to completion, largely because the project involved extensive structural repairs as well as repainting.
* **2005 Repaint** – Completed within nine months after a six‑month preparatory phase.
* **2019–2020 Maintenance Cycle** – Planned for 11 months, reflecting modern safety regulations and more stringent environmental controls.

These timelines illustrate how much of the effort lies outside the mere act of spraying paint.

---

### Rough Numbers You Can Use

If you’re curious about raw math:

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Height | 330 m (1083 ft) |
| Approx. surface area | 10 000 m² (~107 500 sq ft) |
| Paint required | ~30 kg/m² → ~300 t of paint |
| Crew size | 20–25 skilled painters + support staff |
| Daily output per painter | 50–70 m²/day (depending on equipment) |
| Total days needed (pure painting) | 150–180 days (≈ 5–6 months) |

Add the other phases above, and you get the full year‑long cycle.

---

#### Bottom line

While the physical act of applying paint covers a relatively short period, the whole operation—from regulatory paperwork through cleanup—spans close to a year. That’s why the Eiffel Tower receives its fresh coat approximately every seven to eight years, giving enough time for careful maintenance without disrupting tourism too heavily.
